✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: Simple and clean contribution. Can be done quickly in any language available. It's also a great Reverse mode exercise as it expects basic ASCII code knowledge.

I like the contribution. It's pretty simple and it can be done in 14 lines of C code.
But there's two problems:

1. Why can't this be a fastest mode clash? I think it's perfectly suitable for it.

2. Why specify the number of characters the input string has? Every programming language available in the IDE of Clash of Code has a way of getting the length of the string using a function or attribute (Like `strlen` in C, `len` in Python or `.length` in JS/TS). Removing the input containing the length of `n` will make the contribution cleaner and possibly avoiding a red herring when in Reverse mode.

You can check languages and versions at
https://www.codingame.com/playgrounds/40701/help-center/languages-versions

[Goal]

- Please add "... average ASCII code (rounded down) of all lowercase ..." to the problem description.

[Input]

- I agree with @nicof6786's suggestion, but please move the line "[[s]] contains only letters" into the Constraints section instead.

- Please consider adding the length of string s as part of the input; e.g.:

5
nNeoc

This will help players who code in languages which do not automatically support parsing of variable-length inputs, especially in Reverse mode.

[Cases]

- Consider adding one or two more non-trivial cases and then reordering the cases, such that the solution is not immediately obvious in Reverse mode.

Thank you!

What language in this platform doesn't support parsing variable-length inputs?

@jonas_melo Apologies, I was under the impression that languages requiring explicit memory allocation (e.g. C) would risk undefined behaviour if the length was not specified. Glad to know strlen does the trick.

Regarding input format, specifying both the length of the input with the input itself is a common format and is unlikely to be misinterpreted. But since it's easier to parse the input without the input length, I'm happy to leave the input format as-is :)

Actually, @User123's concern is understandable. In C, reading arbitrary-length input into a fixed-size buffer without bounds checking can indeed lead to undefined behaviour (e.g. buffer overflows). strlen doesn't solve that problem. So, while the input doesn't need to explicitly include the string length, it's still good practice to include it as an input, otherwise the problem statement must specify an upper bound on the string length. That allows implementations in languages like C to allocate buffers safely or choose an appropriate dynamic allocation strategy.

Got it, but every problem in CoC that reads a line needs an upper bound in the stub. If you put 10 as the bound and add a test case with a text of size of 20, the platform reports an error at you. So it's impossible to have buffer overflows and strlen will always work on that buffer correctly.
The problem statement doesn't specify the upper bound, but the constraint section do. Also, the C code generated by the stub reads from stdin into a buffer of correct size.
I meant for the player, not for the author.
Also I'm sorry for the confusion. I used the term "problem statement" loosely as I was thinking of it including all the sections, including the Constraints section.
Oh, I'm sorry 🤦‍♂️. I still need to work on my english interpretation.
